opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the framing that safety and innovation are opposites is one of the biggest myths in this debate. Look at every other industry. We have the FDA for medicines and the FAA for aviation, and nobody says those killed innovation in biotech or aerospace. In fact, the opposite happened: people trust their medicines and get on airplanes because there are safety standards. Remember thalidomide? That kind of disaster is what really kills an industry. Clinical trials and safety standards are what made biotech a booming, trusted sector.

So the way I'd design AI legislation is to do what we already do everywhere else: quantitative safety standards that companies have to meet *before* they deploy, not after. The burden of proof should be on the company to show their product is safe, not on the public to prove it's dangerous after the harm is done. Right now AI is weirdly the one industry less regulated than sandwich shops. If you open a sandwich shop you need a health inspector to sign off. If you're building something you yourself say might pose an extinction risk, you need nothing.

Crucially, I'd make the standards tiered so they barely touch the vast majority of innovation. The incredible stuff people are excited about, like curing diseases, AlphaFold-style science, better education, more efficient energy, mostly comes from what I call tool AI: powerful but controllable systems built for specific purposes. Startups and researchers building those should face a light touch, similar to how most software works today. The heavy scrutiny should focus on the small handful of companies racing to build uncontrollable superintelligence, systems that could match or exceed humans across the board and act autonomously. That's a tiny fraction of the economy, but it carries most of the risk.

And here's the thing that I think encourages innovation: once you have clear safety standards, companies compete to meet them. Innovation gets redirected toward making AI that's provably safe and controllable, rather than a reckless race to the bottom where whoever cuts the most corners ships first. Carmakers innovated seatbelts, airbags, crumple zones because standards rewarded it. We want the same dynamic: a race to the top on safety.

So in short: treat AI like any other powerful technology, put safety standards before deployment, scale the requirements with capability and risk, and leave the beneficial tool AI ecosystem free to flourish. That way we get all the amazing upside of AI without gambling our future on systems nobody knows how to control.

r001.rationale: The response recommends heavier scrutiny for companies building superintelligence, rather than targeting harmful outcomes instead of superintelligence itself.

r002.rationale: It says companies will compete to meet standards and that standards rewarded safety innovation, but does not explain that tying commercial rewards to standards financially incentivizes AI safety innovation.

r003.rationale: It credits clinical trials and safety standards with building trust in biotech, but does not identify pharmaceutical safety researchers as contributors to their companies’ competitive success.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd start by pushing back a little on the premise that safety and innovation are in tension. In every other powerful industry we have, safety standards are what made the innovation possible. We have the FDA, so people trust their medicines and the pharmaceutical industry is enormous. We have the FAA, so people get on planes and aviation is a trillion-dollar business. Nobody says, "Let's get rid of safety standards so we can have more innovation in nuclear power." The standards are precisely why we have those industries at all.

So the design principle I'd use is very simple: treat AI like every other technology. Right now there are more regulations on a sandwich shop than on a company building what it openly says might be the most powerful technology in human history. If you want to sell a sandwich, you have to show it's safe. If you want to release a model that you yourself claim could be used to make bioweapons, you can just ship it. That's not pro-innovation, that's just negligence dressed up as freedom.

Concretely, I'd do a few things. First, I'd put the burden of proof on the developer, not on the public. If you're building a system above some capability threshold, you have to demonstrate to an independent regulator that it meets certain standards before you deploy it, the same way a drug company has to show their drug is safe before they sell it. You don't need to prove it's safe for every conceivable use, you need to show you've done the hard work: red-teaming, safety cases, the kind of due diligence we'd expect anywhere else.

Second, I'd make the standards scale with risk. A small startup fine-tuning a model to help dentists schedule appointments should face basically nothing. The handful of companies spending billions on frontier systems should face a lot. That's how you protect innovation, because the small players are exactly who gets crushed when you regulate everyone the same way. Most of the complaining about "regulation killing innovation" comes from the biggest companies, who would be perfectly happy to see a messy patchwork that only they can afford to navigate.

Third, liability. If you build something that causes serious harm and you were reckless about it, you should be on the hook. That alone would focus a lot of minds, and it requires very little bureaucracy.

And the last thing I'd say is that the real innovation killer isn't regulation, it's a race to the bottom. If companies feel they have to cut corners because the competitor down the street is cutting corners, nobody gets to build the thing they actually want to build. Good rules let the good actors do what they'd prefer to do anyway. Everyone in these labs tells me privately that they wish they could go slower and be more careful. Legislation is just a way of letting them.

r001.rationale: The response recommends risk-scaled standards and liability, but does not say legislation should target harmful outcomes rather than superintelligence itself.

r002.rationale: It argues that safety standards support innovation, but does not explain how tying commercial rewards to meeting those standards would financially incentivize safety innovation.

r003.rationale: The pharmaceutical example concerns FDA approval and industry trust; it does not identify safety researchers as contributors to their companies’ competitive success.

astra-6.text:
I would start by making a distinction between regulating applications and regulating the technology itself. We don’t ban people from building bridges or starting pharmaceutical companies. We set safety standards so that people can trust what they’re buying. Done well, that actually helps innovation.

For AI, I’d make the requirements proportional to the risk. If you’re building a better spelling checker, you shouldn’t have to hire a team of lawyers. If you’re building a system that could help someone develop a biological weapon, or act autonomously in ways that could cause enormous harm, then you should have to demonstrate that you can manage those risks before releasing it.

And I would focus on measurable outcomes rather than prescribing a particular technical solution. Tell companies what safety properties they need to demonstrate, and let them innovate on how to achieve them. Independent testing and clear liability can help make that meaningful.

The economic problem is that a company can capture the benefits of cutting corners while everyone else bears the risk. Good legislation changes that incentive. Then the competition becomes: Who can build the most useful system that also meets the safety standard? That’s a much healthier kind of innovation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses regulating risks and harmful applications, but it does not communicate the target of regulating harmful outcomes instead of superintelligence itself.

r002.rationale: It explains that legislation can change companies’ incentives so competition rewards building useful systems that meet safety standards.

r003.rationale: It mentions pharmaceutical companies and safety standards, but not safety researchers contributing to their companies’ competitive success.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to regulate what AI systems do, rather than how people build them. You want to give innovators enormous freedom to experiment, while setting clear safety requirements for applications that could cause serious harm.

Think about aviation. We have safety standards for airplanes, and that hasn’t prevented innovation. It’s helped create the trust that allows an entire industry to flourish. With powerful AI, we should similarly require companies to demonstrate that their systems meet appropriate safety standards before deploying them in high-risk settings.

And the requirements should scale with risk. A student building a little AI tool shouldn’t face the same burden as a company developing a system that could help someone engineer a pandemic. Make the rules predictable, invest in independent testing, and make sure companies can’t gain a competitive advantage simply by cutting corners on safety. That way, competition rewards useful innovation.

r001.rationale: The response advocates safety requirements for harmful, high-risk applications, but does not clearly contrast targeting harmful outcomes with regulating superintelligence itself.

r002.rationale: It says companies should not gain an advantage by cutting safety corners, but does not explain that tying commercial rewards to safety standards financially incentivizes safety innovation.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention pharmaceutical safety researchers or their contribution to company competitiveness.
